en: The Sūtra on the Divine Incantation of the Bodhisattva Gaganagañja Spoken by the Buddha.

Thus have I heard: At one time the Buddha was dwelling on Mount Kāliṅgavana at the abode of sages and seers, together with a great assembly of countless bhikṣus and a multitude of great bodhisattvas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Having finished expounding the *Sūtra on the Boundless Measure of the Tathāgata’s Virtues*,
at that time, a wish-fulfilling jewel appeared spontaneously in the western direction,
with hundreds of thousands of Śakrābhilagna jewels serving as its retinue.
The light emitted by that wish-fulfilling jewel was all-pervasively penetrating;

all the light, colors, and forms of the four great elements belonging to the humans, devas, śrāvakas, and bodhisattvas here were extinguished without remainder. With the exception of the Tathāgata and the wish-fulfilling jewel, everything else shared the same characteristics as immeasurable, boundless, and ineffable space.
At that time, the World-Honored One’s radiance became even more brilliant.
The sentient beings in the assembly could no longer see one another, nor could they perceive the touch, color, or physical forms of their bodies.
In whatever direction they looked, they could not see the light of the sun, moon, or stars.

The eyes do not see forms, the ears do not hear sounds, the nose does not smell fragrances, the tongue does not perceive tastes, and the body does not feel tactile objects; as for the mind and its mental factors, there is neither self nor what belongs to a self—there is only the vision of the Tathāgata’s physical marks, radiance, and wish-fulfilling jewel.

The bodhisattvas present in the assembly—those dwelling in the ten stages, those who have attained the Śūraṅgama Samādhi, those in their last birth before buddhahood, and those in their final body—felt no fear in their hearts.
Why is this? It is because they have understood the jewel-like characteristic of the *tathatā* (suchness) of all phenomena, which is the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*).

Consequently, the other bodhisattvas, the assembly of śrāvakas, and the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, kiṃnaras, gandharvas, piśācas, pūtanas, kaṭapūtanas, humans, and non-humans who had gathered there were all struck with terror; some could not even perceive one another, wondering, "What is this?"
There was no one to ask about this.
At that time, there was a bodhisattva mahāsattva in the assembly named Brahma-voice (Brahmaghoṣa), who rose from his seat, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and spoke these verses:
“The true meaning of all phenomena, Sentient beings are unable to know it.”
Because fools among the six sense bases crave and cling to the aggregate of form,
they fail to see even a single aggregate and instead seek out the characteristics of form.
Now there are such people who harbor doubts regarding the Buddha-dharma.
I only pray that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, will explain the true nature for me,
so that I may understand this and that, and swiftly realize the patience that is like space.
O valiant hero of meditative concentration, your body is beyond description.
The wish-fulfilling maṇi jewel appears upon his crown; Śākyalaṅkābha is not far away.
Those sentient beings who come shall, with heroic vigor, reach the further shore.
All possess great wisdom and desire to come and see the World-Honored One;
he will surely preach the most profound Dharma, of which there is no doubt.
We only pray that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, will comfort all those who have gathered here.
"Bringing accomplishment to sentient beings—this is the practice of a Great Being.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Just as you have said, it is brought about by the power of samādhi."
Only those who possess wisdom can hear of this matter:
the practice of the Great Being, the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha, which is without dependence and free from conceptual proliferation; such is the power of his samādhi.
Firmly adhering to these two views is the conduct of the deluded and confused;
because they cling to annihilationism and eternalism, they do not understand this or that.
If one wishes to attain liberation from these two views, [one must abandon them].
"One should not be attached to various desires, so as to swiftly realize the various stages.
The Buddha told Brahmā-svara: "Good son!..."

For a bodhisattva who has newly begun their practice, one should first teach that there are conditioned perceptions for practicing the six pāramitās. Once they can understand that the nature of the four great elements is a phenomenon of arising and ceasing, one may then teach that all dharmas are ineffable, devoid of self-characteristics, neither arising nor ceasing, without conditions, and non-existent; that all conditioned formations are likewise thus.

One who can contemplate in this way is free from the views of annihilationism and eternalism, and is likewise without fear. Being without conditions or contact regarding all phenomena, one is able to swiftly fulfill the six pāramitās, while also remaining unattached to various views such as annihilationism and eternalism.
"By the Buddha's spiritual power, let all those gathered here in this great assembly see, hear, perceive, and know exactly as before.
At that time, the World-Honored One raised his right hand and addressed the great assembly, saying:

"The Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha has now come from there. This Bodhisattva’s meditative concentration is like the ocean; his pure precepts are like a mountain; his wisdom is like space; his diligence is like the wind; his patience is like a diamond; and his insight is like the sands of the Ganges. He is the banner of all Bodhisattvas and the guide for those heading toward Nirvana. He is a river and pond of roots of goodness, a precious vase for the poor, the sun for those in darkness, the moon for those who have lost their way, a mountain for those in fear, and a potent medicine for those afflicted by the disease of afflictions."
It purifies the water of all views and subdues all demonic adversaries, like frost and lightning that clear away impurities; it is like the añjana medicine for those who have violated the precepts.

It is the ground for all roots of goodness, a garland amidst the various flowers, a mirror for those who act wickedly, and eyes for those lacking shame and remorse. It is a skilled physician for the sick, a bed and seat for the weary and exhausted; it can satisfy hunger like Śrī-devī and remove thirst like the moonstone, and it illuminates those in meditative concentration like the sunstone.

For those practicing the path to Bodhi, it is a chariot; for those sporting in meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), it is a pond; for those cultivating the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*), it is a floral garland; for those practicing the various *pāramitās*, it is a wondrous fruit; for those illuminating the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), it is a wish-fulfilling jewel (*cintāmaṇi*); for those dwelling in the Śūraṅgama Samādhi, it is like a Pārijātaka tree; for severing the fetters of all views, it is like a sharp blade; for removing habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), it is like a diamond (*vajra*); and for its wisdom in subduing the enmity of Māra, it is like a fierce fire.

His body is the vessel for the teachings of all Buddhas; he is a floral garland for pratyekabuddhas, a robe for śrāvakas, the eyes of the devas, the true guide for humanity, the refuge for animals, the destination for hungry ghosts, and the vessel for the Dharma that protects sentient beings in the hells.

The Bodhisattva Banya serves as an attendant to the Buddhas of the three periods of time, guarding the gates of the Dharma-city; he has already been able to adorn himself with the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha and is endowed with all-encompassing wisdom.
This son of noble family deserves the most supreme offerings from all sentient beings, with the sole exception of the Tathāgata.

All of you who have gathered here should approach him and, according to your own capacity, offer him worship, respect, honor, and praise; with various precious gems, jeweled banners, pennants, canopies, flowers, incense, and necklaces, you should purify and adorn the roads. Before long, you too shall become such vessels of the Dharma.

At that time, the entire assembly gathered there rose from their seats, joined their palms in reverence, and facing the direction from which the Bodhisattva Gaganagañja had come, they paid homage with joy, gazing upon him without weariness.

At that time, within the assembly, the great Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, as well as the great Śrāvakas, the kings of the devas, the kings of the nāgas, the kings of the yakṣas, the kings of the asuras, the kings of the garuḍas, the kings of the kiṃnaras, the kings of the mahoragas, and the rishis possessing the five supernatural powers, all had this thought:
"With what most excellent offerings should we present to honor and make offerings to that son of good family?"

At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Ākāśagarbha immediately transformed this Sahā world so that it was devoid of mountains, wildernesses, mounds, valleys, or ravines; he removed all foul odors, filth, dust, and harsh sounds.
He manifested trees made of the seven precious substances, whose flowers and fruits emitted subtle and wondrous fragrances, while all grasses and trees upon the earth became the seven treasures.

All the sickness and suffering of sentient beings, as well as the sufferings of the hells, were entirely extinguished. Clothing, food, drink, and various ornaments were provided according to their wishes; their physical forms became upright and handsome, their faculties were complete, they were free from afflictions, their minds were tranquil, and they delighted in cultivating roots of goodness with deep faith in the Triple Gem.

Among all those who had gathered in the assembly, every single sentient being held a wish-fulfilling jewel in each of their two hands; from each of these jewels issued forth light that illuminated the Sahā world, making it brilliantly radiant everywhere.

Exquisite celestial music of various sounds resounded, and there rained down diverse heavenly garments, necklaces, flowers, and fruits, as well as *tamarapaṭa* and ox-head sandalwood, along with powdered incense of various kinds contained in exquisite vessels.
On both sides of that road, precious halls were manifested, resembling the Vaijayanta Hall of Śakra.
Within those halls were all majestic celestial maidens, like the exquisite court ladies of the Sixth Heavenly King, performing celestial music.
In the space above the World-Honored One’s head was a great precious canopy, one hundred yojanas in length and breadth, adorned with various jewels like a Brahma-canopy;
nets of various jewels, interlaced with golden threads and pearls, all produced celestial music.

From the earth grew grasses, trees, flowers, fruits, branches, and leaves, from which celestial music also issued; the sounds all expounded the Mahāyāna True Dharma and the six pāramitās, and all sentient beings who heard them attained non-retrogression from anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

At that time, the great assembly, seeing the Bodhisattva Gaganagañja manifest such magnificent adornments, felt in their hearts a joy and wonder never before experienced, and they all spoke these words:
"By what means shall we prepare a Dharma-seat before the World-Honored One, so that this son of noble family may sit upon it?"

At that time, a great lotus flower appeared spontaneously before the Buddha, ten *li* in length and breadth, with a stem of white silver, petals of gold, a pedestal of agate, and filaments of Brahma-light jewels; furthermore, there were hundreds of thousands of such lotus flowers surrounding it.
The Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha sat cross-legged upon a lotus flower, with a wish-fulfilling jewel atop his head.
All the members of the retinue brought by the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha likewise sat upon lotus flowers.
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva addressed the Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja with these verses:
"Of all the bodhisattvas who have appeared in the past, Those who possessed great renown First paid homage to the Buddha,
the World-Honored One, And only thereafter took their seats."
"Now these great beings, manifesting wondrously adorned deeds,
do not even pay homage to the World-Honored One, but instead immediately take their seats.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyarāja answered the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Maitreya with a verse:
"This Great Being now abides in the profound Dharma of the Buddha;
he perceives no sentient beings and does not discriminate his own self.
Maitreya Bodhisattva again asked in verse:
"If you do not perceive sentient beings, you must abide in the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
For what reason do you manifest such adornments?
I pray that you answer with certainty."
Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja replied again in verse:
“The one of courageous skillful means seeks to bring sentient beings to fulfillment.
The ignorant and foolish act with conceptual discrimination, failing to understand the meaning of reality.”
"Knowing only the conventional truth, one suffers because of failing to realize the ultimate.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the son of good family: "Excellent!"
Excellent! As you have said, all ordinary beings cannot know the skillful means and liberation of even a single *srotāpanna*.
Even if all sentient beings were *srotāpannas*, they could not know the skillful means and liberation of even a single *sakṛdāgāmin*.
Just as a Sakṛdāgāmin, Anāgāmin, or Arhat cannot know the skillful means and liberation of a single Pratyekabuddha;

so too all sentient beings—who are like Pratyekabuddhas throughout an entire kalpa—cannot know the skillful means, the maturing of sentient beings, and the liberation of a single Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who has attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

Although all sentient beings have attained the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), they are unable to know the skillful means and liberations of those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who have attained the *śūraṅgama-samādhi* and possess unimpeded wisdom that penetrates the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).

This Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Ākāśagarbha has already passed through immeasurable and boundless kalpas, attaining the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), all unhindered knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), and the Śūraṅgama Samādhi; having penetrated the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), he is fully able to know the mental activities and afflictions of all those gathered in this assembly.
There may be sentient beings who, upon seeing these great adornments and subtle wonders, all attain the stage of freedom from desire.

This son of noble family passes away from that place and appears here, manifesting through the supernatural powers, wisdom, and samādhis of space, causing all sentient beings to give rise to a mind of weary detachment; thereafter, he further manifests the samādhi of worldly-adornment, enabling immeasurable sentient beings to achieve such a samādhi as is not shared with śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.

If that son of noble family manifests the adornment of the ultimate truth of non-arising, all humans, devas, and even Bodhisattvas up to the eighth stage will be struck with wonder and doubt, unable to comprehend the characteristics of his conduct.

Such are the merits of these profound Buddha-dharmas; by means of skillful wisdom, that son of noble family, within the ocean of all Buddha-dharmas, has no doubt in his mind and does not rely on others for knowledge. Among all the secret dharmas of the Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, he is like a supreme banner, able to show sentient beings the path of goodness and the path to nirvāṇa, and able to cure the mental illnesses of afflictions as well as the physical illnesses of sentient beings.

There are sentient beings who, in the vast wilderness of birth and death, are submerged by false views and are unable to know the skillful means for proceeding toward the good realms and nirvana; such persons should always, with a profound mind, recite the name of the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha, prostrate to him with reverence, and make offerings by burning agalloch incense.
That son of good family observes his defiled mind and afflictions; according to those afflictions, various views, and ignorance,
as well as his previously cultivated roots of goodness and his disciplined mind, he plants roots of goodness in the presence of the Buddha,
the Dharma, and the Sangha, or performs meritorious deeds through giving and meritorious deeds through maintaining the precepts.
Cultivating the meritorious karma of meditative concentration, according to what is appropriate for each, whether in dreams or while awake,
he reveals the right path through great skillful means. By means of these correct skillful means, he causes those sentient beings to swiftly abandon wrong views, wrong conduct, wrong aspirations,
wrong thoughts, and wrong destinies, leading their bodies, speech, and minds toward right practice and right action.
May good friends swiftly be able to eliminate defiled and evil afflictions, leave behind all evil realms,
not destroy wholesome causes, and attain mastery of mind, abiding in profound patience.

If there are sentient beings who suffer from various physical ailments, insanity, mental derangement, blindness, inability to speak, or bodily deformities, they should, with a profound mind, invoke the name of the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha. To eliminate these illnesses, they should burn agarwood or tagara incense while prostrating and making offerings.

That son of good family, within his dream, will see hosts of Brahmā deities, or the elephant of Śakra, or the elephant of Śrī-devī, or the elephant of Sārasvata-deva, or the elephant of a kṣatriya, or the elephant of a great minister, or the elephant of his father and mother, or the elephant of his sons and daughters standing before him; they will manifest the appropriate remedies and necessary items according to what is required, so that by means of these, the patient's illness may be extinguished without remainder.
If there are those who are exhorted to seek wealth and possessions; those who study to seek extensive learning; those who practice seated meditation to seek wisdom;
those who seek fame and reputation; those who seek skillful arts; those who seek villages and settlements; those who seek nobility and high status;
those who seek physical beauty and strength; those who seek noble lineage; those who seek a melodious voice; or those who seek to be male—
As for her female retinue: those who seek generosity and ethical discipline up to wisdom; those who seek a sublime voice so that the multitude may delight in hearing it;
those who wish to distance themselves from evil; those who wish to cause others to abide in generosity up to wisdom;
those who wish to attain long life; and those who wish to ensure their means of livelihood do not perish—[they all] desired...
May those who are stingy cultivate relinquishment; may those who violate the precepts abide in the precepts; may those who are indolent apply themselves with diligence;
may those with distorted wisdom attain right wisdom; may those who have not yet entered the Vehicle enter the Vehicle.

For those who seek the Vehicle for themselves, those who seek the Vehicle for others, those who lack great compassion, and those who do not act for their own sake but only for the sake of sentient beings—by what means...?

One should pay homage and show reverence to the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha, who employs skillful means to cause these sentient beings not to regress from Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and to abide in the four immeasurable minds of great skillful means.

Whether in an open space or within a grove, if one burns tagara incense or katu-arura incense, joins the palms in reverence toward the ten directions, and having paid homage, should recite this mantra:
*Tadyathā | amṛte amṛte | kaṃkari kaṭa kaṭa vi-kaṭa kaṭa saṃkaṭa kaṃkari* (with the *nu* sound reversed).

The remainder is the same as [the mantra] beginning with *khaṃ harama harama vigā arimamarmadharmabuddhajaṣṭamaṇakajañjane jantamaṇe nukīcara nyakajañjane saravāsajinhami svāhā vadya ahyenaraha arisadgaṅga saṅga saṅga huṃ kṛti dumi*.

Hya bi hya ju mi gha hya kung t'ung hya ti tu er li shih chi hya ju gha hya kung t'ung hya ka tsung ni ka t'ung hya lien li yeh tou mo a shia t'ung hya yeh sa lo po p'o t'o chieh a shu kia gha ti sa svāhā. "If one can thus recite and uphold this mantra,
whether that son of noble family takes human form or the form of birds and beasts..."
He manifests himself to those people and preaches the Dharma to them according to their respective merits.
He demonstrates a single skillful means.

By means of this one skillful means, he is able to cause hundreds of thousands of nayutas of sentient beings to come and abide in a vehicle—whether they abide in the vehicle of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas—and by means of a brief application of skillful means, causes them to abide in the non-retrogressive, unsurpassed Mahāyāna, whereby they attain various samādhis, dhāraṇīs, patiences, and stages.
That son of good family possesses inconceivable great skillful means and wisdom, and has accomplished great compassion.

While there may be sentient beings who can measure the limits of space, there is no one who can measure the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha’s great skillful means and wisdom, his great kindness and great compassion, or his power of meditative concentration and samādhi in bringing sentient beings to maturity.
That son of noble family has accomplished such inconceivable and manifold virtuous merits.

If there are sentient beings whose minds are upright and sincere, free from flattery and crookedness, who abide in right view, who do not exalt themselves nor disparage others, who are free from stinginess and envy, and whose minds are pure and without hypocrisy—the sons of noble family, out of compassion for them, shall instruct them to be diligent, demonstrating the correct means so that those sentient beings, through the power of such diligence and these means, may be freed from all misfortunes and afflictions. They shall enable them to resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, dedicate all roots of goodness toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* without falling back, and through the power of such skillful means and diligence, fully fulfill the six *pāramitās*. By practicing diligence with such vigor, they shall swiftly achieve *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
“Ākāśagarbha Bodhisattva has accomplished such inconceivable merit and, through diligent and energetic practice, brings sentient beings to maturity.
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"For what reason, World-Honored One, does this son of good family alone have a wish-fulfilling jewel upon the crown of his head, while the other bodhisattvas do not?
The Buddha told Maitreya:

"This Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha has perfected great compassion. For those who are in perilous suffering, who have committed root transgressions, who are heading toward the evil realms, and whose roots of goodness are incinerated and destroyed—among such beings, he is a supreme medicine. For beings dwelling in darkness, he acts as a great illumination, like the shining of the sun."

If there are sentient beings who have committed root transgressions, with the arrow of doubt lodged in their hearts, thereby destroying the vessel of the Dharma, they will fall forever into ruin and lose their roots of goodness; destined for the evil realms, without refuge or reliance, and abandoned by the wise as wicked beings—those sons of noble family are able to show them the right path, extinguishing their afflictions and causing them to leave the evil realms behind.

If there are sentient beings who abound in greed, anger, and delusion; who claim that cause and effect do not exist and fear nothing of the future world; who amass wealth without satiety and constantly practice greed and envy; and who even exclusively commit the ten unwholesome deeds and incite others to do the same—those sons of noble family, like ships or carts, are able to show them the path of goodness and the path to Nirvana.
"Therefore, that son of good family, with the exception of the Tathāgata, should be honored by all people in the world, including devas and humans.
At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
What constitutes a root offense?

If there are sentient beings who commit a root offense, they burn away their roots of goodness and head toward the evil realms; they fall forever into ruin and loss, deprived of the joys of humans and devas. How, then, can those sons of noble family eliminate such offenses and be sufficed with the joy of the virtuous path and the bliss of nirvana?
The Buddha told Maitreya:

"A Kṣatriya king has five root offenses. If a Kṣatriya king commits these offenses, his roots of goodness will be incinerated and he will head toward the evil realms, falling forever into ruin and deprivation, far removed from the happiness of humans and devas."
What are these five?
If a Kṣatriya king takes property belonging to the Buddha or property belonging to the Saṃgha of the four quarters, or instructs others to take it, this is called the first offense.
To slander the Dharma of the Śrāvakas, the Dharma of the Pratyekabuddhas, or the Mahāyāna Dharma, and to create obstacles by concealing, hiding, or covering them up, is the second offense.

If one has faith and leaves the household life, shaving off hair and beard and donning dyed robes—whether they maintain the precepts or not—to strip them of their *kāṣāya*, compel them to return to secular life, imprison them, inflict corporal punishment, or even take their lives, this is the third offense.

If one commits the five heinous crimes—killing one’s father, killing one’s mother, killing an arhat, causing a schism in the Saṃgha, or with an evil mind drawing blood from the body of a Buddha—and if one performs even one of these five karmas, this constitutes the fourth offense.

To slander the existence of cause and effect and fearlessness toward future lives, constantly practicing the ten unwholesome karmas oneself and teaching others to do so, and personally remaining steadfastly committed while teaching others to remain steadfastly committed to the ten unwholesome karmas—this is the fifth offense.

If a Kṣatriya king commits even one of these five offenses, that Kṣatriya king will burn away his roots of goodness and head toward the evil realms; he will fall forever into ruin and loss, deprived of the happiness of humans and devas.

For the sake of such persons, that son of noble family takes birth in a Licchavi body; he may assume the appearance and deportment of a śramaṇa, or the appearance and deportment of a brāhmaṇa. He speaks to the kṣatriya king concerning the profound and unprecedented sūtras taught by the Omniscient One, as well as various dhāraṇīs, the various patiences (kṣāntis), and the stages (bhūmis). He causes the kṣatriya king to confess his transgressions and cultivate the precepts, so that by hearing of concentration and wisdom and practicing with diligent effort, he may be reborn in a favorable realm.
“Ministers and high officials have five fundamental offenses.
What are these five?
If a minister or high official takes property belonging to the Buddha or property belonging to the Saṃgha, this is called the first offense.”
To destroy cities and villages and to harm the people is the second offense.
To slander the true Dharma as described above is the third offense.
To revile those who have left the household life and cause them suffering, as explained in detail above, is the fourth offense.
To commit even one of the five deeds of immediate retribution is the fifth offense.
"Regarding these five crimes, if a great minister or counselor commits even one such as those described above,
'A śrāvaka disciple has five kinds of root offenses.'"
What are the five? First, killing; second, stealing; third, sexual misconduct; fourth, false speech; and fifth, maliciously drawing blood from the body of a Buddha.
If a śrāvaka disciple commits even one of these five offenses, the consequences are as previously described.

"A beginner bodhisattva has eight root transgressions that destroy the Mahāyāna, incinerate their roots of goodness, and lead them toward evil destinies; they will fall forever into ruin and loss, be deprived of the bliss of the Mahāyāna of humans and devas, and dwell long in saṃsāra, separated from virtuous friends."
What are these eight?

Because of their evil conduct, these sentient beings were born into this perilous and wicked world of the five turbidities; yet, because they possess a small measure of roots of goodness, they draw near to virtuous friends and are able to hear the profound Mahāyāna sūtras.

That person, possessing shallow wisdom and meager roots of goodness, has resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and is a beginner bodhisattva; having heard the exposition of profound sūtras on the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*), he receives, maintains, reads, and recites them exactly as he has heard them.
For those of shallow understanding, one explains the Dharma according to the meanings they have heard.

When such persons hear the Dharma, fear arises in their minds; they then retreat from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and give rise to the mind of a *śrāvaka*. This constitutes a root offense for a beginner Bodhisattva.

Because of committing this offense, one burns away one's roots of goodness and heads toward the evil realms; one falls forever into ruin and loss, becoming separated from the bliss of humans, devas, and nirvāṇa, and destroys the bodhicitta.
Therefore, a bodhisattva should first understand the mental activities of sentient beings and then gradually teach them the Dharma accordingly.

Just as one enters the ocean by degrees until it becomes ever deeper, for the sake of such individuals, the Bodhisattva Gaganagañja assumes bodies in various places so that bodhisattvas who have newly begun their practice may, upon committing transgressions, fear falling into the evil realms.

If one hears the name of the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha and, having heard it, rejoices with the desire to behold him, repents of the transgressions committed, and then, during the latter part of the night, burns agallochum and tagara incense while joining the palms in reverence and reciting the name of the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha.

That son of noble family manifests various bodies according to what is appropriate—whether manifesting his own body, the body of Brahmā or Śakra, or even the bodies of men and women—and appears before those individuals. He causes beginner bodhisattvas to repent and eliminate their transgressions according to their offenses; he further expounds for them the unsurpassed Mahāyāna, the profound skillful means, samādhis, dhāraṇīs, the various patiences (*kṣānti*), and the various stages (*bhūmi*). This enables them to leave behind the terrors of the evil realms, prevents them from regressing from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and inspires in them great vigor like a diamond, so that they may practice the six *pāramitās* and swiftly realize *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
If the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha does not manifest his form, one should supplicate Aruṇa, speaking these words:
"Namo Aruṇa! You have accomplished great compassion and possess great majestic power."

When he appears, may his radiance shine throughout Jambudvīpa and illuminate my own body; I pray that you convey my words to the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha so that I may behold him within my dreams, and that he may show me the skillful means to repent for my fundamental grave offenses, enabling me to attain the noble eye of Mahāyāna wisdom.

At that time, they should sleep in their original place; when the dawn appears, the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha will manifest in their dreams for the sake of beginner bodhisattvas, preaching the skillful means of great wisdom to cause them to repent their transgressions.

Furthermore, they shall not forget the bodhicitta; having attained samādhi and firmly abiding in the Mahāyāna, they will swiftly fulfill the six pāramitās and before long attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
This is called the first offense of a beginner bodhisattva.
"If a beginner bodhisattva says to sentient beings:
'You are unable to skillfully cultivate the prajñāpāramitā of the Mahāyāna, nor can you attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.'"
"You should quickly resolve upon the mind of a śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha; you can then quickly attain liberation from birth and death.
The rest is as explained above; this is called the second offense of a beginner bodhisattva.
"Furthermore, if a beginner bodhisattva says to others:
'Why do you so strictly uphold the prātimokṣa precepts?
You should quickly resolve to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and read and recite the Mahāyāna sūtras.'"
"If, because of afflictions, one gives rise to unwholesome karma of body, speech, and mind, one must eliminate them all so as not to undergo their retribution.
The rest is as explained above; this is called the third offense of a beginner bodhisattva.
"Furthermore, if a beginner bodhisattva says to sentient beings:
'Noble son! You should not listen to or receive the sūtras and teachings of the śrāvakas; you should conceal them.'"
Why is this? Because it cannot enable you to attain the great fruit of retribution or to permanently sever the afflictions.
You should listen to and receive the Mahāyāna sūtras, so that all your evil deeds may be completely extinguished and you may swiftly realize anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"If those sentient beings accept such a view, they commit a root offense; this is called the fourth offense of a beginner bodhisattva.
Furthermore, if a beginner bodhisattva, for the sake of fame and profit, reads, recites, explains, or interprets Mahāyāna sūtras, saying:
'I am a follower of the Mahāyāna.'"

Seeing others obtain gain, they harbor resentment in their hearts; exalting themselves and disparaging others, out of jealousy they falsely claim for themselves that they have attained superhuman dharmas. Such a person commits a grave offense against the Mahāyāna and will head toward the evil realms, falling forever into ruin and loss.
It is like a person who wishes to enter the great ocean, repairs a ship intending to reach the place of jewels, but whose vessel is wrecked midway and they lose their life.

A beginner bodhisattva is just like this: wishing to enter the ocean of the Mahāyāna, out of jealousy they utter false speech, thereby destroying the ship of faith and severing the life-force of wisdom. This is a fundamental offense committed by a *mahallaka*—an ordinary, petty bodhisattva—and it is called the fifth offense of a beginner bodhisattva.
"Furthermore, son of good family!

In a future age, there will be beginner bodhisattvas, both those who have left the household life and those who remain at home, who shall receive, uphold, read, and recite the profound meaning of emptiness, samādhis, dhāraṇīs, the various patiences and stages, the various acts of adornment practiced by great beings, and the Mahāyāna sūtras."
With such a mind, one should explain it for others, saying:
"These dharmas are what I have realized; out of great compassion, I now explain them for you."
"You should practice; before long, you too shall personally realize and see this profound Dharma.
That person does not say, "I merely recite and explain this profound Dharma for others, but have not yet realized it myself."

They falsely claim that they have attained the Dharma realized by the Buddhas of the three periods, the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, and all the worthy sages—Dharmas whose measure exceeds the great ocean.

This is like someone traveling through a vast wilderness, oppressed by hunger and thirst and utterly exhausted, who approaches a forest of trees in search of food and drink; yet, abandoning the trees of sweet fruit, they go toward poisonous trees and eat their fruit, whereupon they immediately perish.

I say that such a person is likewise: having obtained this body so difficult to find, having encountered a virtuous friend and met with the Mahāyāna Dharma, yet for the sake of craving gain and offerings, they falsely exalt themselves and disparage others.
Such a person commits a root offense and heads toward the evil realms; they fall forever into ruin and loss, held in contempt by the wise.
Such a person should not be associated with.
Whether they be kṣatriyas, brāhmaṇas, vaiśyas, śūdras, or any wise persons, all who associate with them commit an offense.
This is called the sixth offense of a bodhisattva who has newly entered the path.

"Furthermore, son of good family, in a future age there will be kṣatriya kings who have as their state preceptors, ministers, assistants, and high officials *caṇḍālas*, as well as *caṇḍāla* physicians; moreover, there will be those who are foolish yet consider themselves wise, giving rise to great arrogance."

Such people as these, possessing abundant wealth and jewels, extensively cultivate various meritorious deeds of giving; yet because they rely on their practice of giving, they become arrogant and heedless.
They speak of the various faults and evils of the śramaṇas to the kṣatriya kings, and likewise speak of the faults and evils of the kings to the śramaṇas.
Due to the power of the king, he exiled śramaṇas and plundered their property.
At that time, the bhikṣus, being thus oppressed by him, took the property of the Buddha, the property of the Saṃgha of the four quarters, and even their own personal belongings, and gave them to him.
Once the *caṇḍālas* have obtained these items, they present them to such a king; since both parties commit a grave offense, this is called the seventh transgression.

"Furthermore, in future ages there will be wicked kings and *caṇḍāla* śramaṇas who mistake what is not the Dharma for the Dharma. They will abandon the *sūtras*, the *vinaya*, and the true precepts, nor will they rely upon the Prajñāpāramitā precepts taught by the Great Compassionate Teacher—the Black Seal and the Great Seal—nor the precepts of skillful means found in other *sūtras*. Instead, they will create different teachings and establish new regulations to harass and disturb bhikṣus who practice the Dharma. Because of this harassment, those bhikṣus will be unable to cultivate *vipaśyanā* and *śamatha*; instead, they will devote themselves mostly to study and take pleasure in worldly affairs."
Because they engage in such actions, they are unable to subdue their fetters and afflictions.

These bhikṣus have lost their wholesome minds and violated their dignified decorum; their conduct is negligent and indolent. In truth, though not śramaṇas, they claim to be śramaṇas; though not practicing the holy life (brahmacarya), they claim to practice the holy life; they feel no sense of restraint or caution, speaking aloud and in disorder.

It is like one who possesses a fine voice and is skilled at preaching the Dharma, causing Kṣatriya kings and their ministerial aides to respect and make offerings to him; yet he falsely speaks of the various faults and evils of bhikṣus who practice the Dharma to laypeople, causing the kings and ministers to give rise to feelings of resentment and reproach, and taking the requisites and livelihoods of those practicing bhikṣus to bestow them upon householding bhikṣus—such a person commits a grave offense along with those involved.

Why is this? A bhikṣu established in meditative concentration is a field of merit, a vessel for samādhi, dhāraṇī, the various patiences, and the stages; he expounds the right path, acts as a source of illumination, and delivers sentient beings from their afflictions and karmic deeds.
The Buddha has taught these eight root offenses for beginner bodhisattvas who have not yet perfected the Dharma.

If a beginner bodhisattva commits even one of these eight acts, that beginner bodhisattva will burn away their roots of goodness and head toward the evil realms; they will fall forever into ruin and loss, be deprived of the happiness of humans and devas, and destroy the bodhicitta.

"For the sake of such persons, the Bodhisattva Gaganagañja manifests his body in various lands and in every place; he may manifest the appearance and deportment of a śramaṇa, or even the appearance and deportment of an animal, as explained at length in the Śūraṅgama Sūtra. In these places, he expounds for all sentient beings the Tathāgata’s profound sūtras, samādhis, dhāraṇīs, the various patiences (kṣānti), and the stages (bhūmi), causing those beginner bodhisattvas who have committed offenses and lack skillful means to feel shame and remorse, to harbor deep fear, and to openly confess and repent."

If any sentient beings hear the name of the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha and desire to see him in his entirety in order to repent their grave offenses, so that they may forever eliminate the fear of the evil realms, they should pay homage and invoke the name of the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha.

That son of noble family, according to the power of his merit, may manifest his own body, or the body of Brahmā or Śakra, or even the bodies of men or women, appearing before that person. He causes the beginner bodhisattva to repent for whatever offenses they have committed. Furthermore, he expounds for them the unsurpassed Mahāyāna, the profound skillful means, samādhi, and dhāraṇī, causing them to firmly abide in the various patiences (kṣānti) and stages (bhūmi), forever distancing themselves from the terrors of the evil realms, and ensuring they do not regress from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Possessing the great vigor and courageous power like a flash of lightning, they practice the six pāramitās and swiftly achieve *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

"If that son of good family does not appear before him so that he may see him, then that novice bodhisattva who has committed an offense should, during the latter part of the night, face the eastern direction, burn incense, and pay homage while making this petition to the Arūpadeva:

'Homage to the Arūpadeva! You have perfected great compassion and possess great majestic power. When you appear, may your radiance shine throughout Jambudvīpa and illuminate my body. I pray that you convey my words to the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha so that I may see him in a dream; show me the skillful means to repent for my fundamental grave offenses, and grant me the noble eye of Mahāyāna wisdom.'"

At that time, they should sleep in their original place. When the sun rises, the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha will manifest his body within their dreams for the sake of the beginner bodhisattvas, teaching them the skillful means of great wisdom. This shall cause them to repent of their transgressions, so that they never again forget the mind of bodhi; they shall attain samādhi, abide firmly in the Mahāyāna, and swiftly fulfill the six pāramitās.
Before long, he shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Because he possesses such inconceivable great merit of diligent and heroic effort, this wish-fulfilling jewel is upon the crown of the head of the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha.
"Furthermore, son of good family!

If there are sentient beings who hear the name of the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha and draw or paint his image and make offerings to it, wherever such persons are born, fire shall not burn them, water shall not drown them, weapons shall not harm them, and poisons shall not injure them. Neither humans nor non-humans shall be able to assail them, and they shall never die an untimely death;
royal punishments shall not befall them, and they shall not commit root transgressions."
They are free from disease and do not die of starvation.

When their life is about to end—even when the eyes no longer see forms, the ears no longer hear sounds, the nose no longer smells odors, the tongue no longer perceives tastes, and the body no longer feels tactile sensations—there still remains a subtle inhalation and exhalation of breath; a slight consciousness remains in the body until finally, even that subtlest consciousness ceases.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha immediately manifested his body. If these sentient beings had previously served Brahmā, he would manifest in the form of Brahmā; if they had previously served Māra, Nārāyaṇa, Maheśvara, Śakra-devendra, a Cakravartin King, the Sun or Moon Devas, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, or even Vaiśravaṇa—according to whom they had served—he would manifest his body before those individuals and speak this verse:
"These Four Noble Truths are seen by the wise;
By knowing them regarding birth and death, One is able to cross the ocean of all existences."
“At that time, once those sentient beings have understood this Dharma within their mental consciousness, they are all reborn in auspicious realms.
If there are sentient beings who have faith and reverence for the Buddha, the Buddha immediately manifests his own body and speaks these verses:
“The Buddha’s perfect wisdom is pure; He is able to ferry all across the ocean of existence.”
"May they swiftly realize all the stages and be far removed from all suffering.
At that time, when sentient beings heard these words and contemplated the Buddha’s merits, after their lives ended, the lands where they were reborn were pure and free from the five turbidities.
One beholds all the Buddhas preaching the Dharma in the present; the same applies to mindfulness of the Dharma and mindfulness of the Sangha.

The Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha has accomplished such inconceivable and profound merit. If there are sentient beings who wish to attain various forms of mastery over the mind, they should, during the latter part of the night, bathe themselves clean and reverently prostrate before the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha. Raising a heart of compassion for all sentient beings, they should speak these words:
"Think of me, think of me, O Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha, who possesses great wisdom and has attained great compassion!"
"Please grant me the skillful means for mindfulness and concentration (*smṛti-samādhi-yoga*). He then spoke this mantra:

*Tadyathā | huṃ caura ānanda kṣipāmi | tvaṃ nīle samudra pātāle | tannaya mahācaure | kāraṇa-nubhaṃsi | bhañja-mṛty-āgala-bhaṃsa | mṛtyu-bhañja-raṃsi | bhaṃsa-mṛtyu-bhañja-hara-saṃsara-bhañja | ānma-saṃsara-bhañja | putra-kujñi-saṃsara-bhañja | svāhā ||* "If one recites and upholds this mantra, one will immediately attain entry into the skillful means of mindfulness and concentration."
Furthermore, if one wishes to read or recite various sūtras and śāstras—whether spoken by the Buddha or spoken by his disciples—one should bathe and purify oneself;
the rest is as explained above. Then, one should recite the mantra as follows: *Tadyathā | ānīra-jaḥ-ṇi-kam-pu-sa-su-kaja-ṇi-yapana-ja-ṇi-pakṣa-same-paca-raṇa-ra* || 1 ||
*Jaṣa śukaṣa taṇa sara ṇiśa sata laka raṇu humma humma mahākaṅkani ka svāhā.* "If one wishes to enter the great ocean,
or wishes to enter a deep cavern to seek treasures..."
As for those who are different: those wishing to take the elixirs of the immortals; those who are bound and imprisoned; those undergoing punishment; those facing death;
those suffering from separation from loved ones; those encountering the hated and disliked; those fearing water, fire, or weapons;
those plundered by tigers, wolves, lions, venomous snakes, or bandits; and those afflicted by chronic illness or even lacking food and clothing.
One should pay homage and show reverence to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Gaganagañja; the rest is as explained above.

If there are princes who wish to seek the royal throne, those who wish to seek long life, those who wish to seek the majesty of a Brahmin, those who wish to seek the majesty of a householder, those who wish to seek skill in arts and techniques, those who wish to seek renown, those who wish to seek a handsome and upright appearance, those who wish to seek the cultivation of meditative concentration, or those who wish to seek liberation—such sentient beings, upon hearing the name of the Bodhisattva Gaganagañja, should, during the final watch of the night, bathe themselves clean, put on new and fine garments, ascend a high seat, and with a sincere mind, pray for water, speaking these words:
"Homage to the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha!
O you who possess great compassion, grant me merit and fulfill my aspirations.
When that son of noble family hears this with his divine ear, he manifests his form in accordance with the power of that person's merit.
That son of good family possesses such inconceivable great wisdom and skillful means; having perfected all virtuous merits, he has already crossed the vast ocean of the profound Buddha-dharma.
O son of good family!

There may be sentient beings who can count the four great oceans of water and know the number of their drops, yet there are no sentient beings who can measure the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha’s great wisdom and skillful means in bringing sentient beings to maturity;
there may be sentient beings who can measure the boundaries of immeasurable and boundless space, yet there are no sentient beings who can calculate the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Ākāśagarbha.

For the sake of bringing sentient beings to maturity, they manifest various bodies—whether as the body of a Buddha, the body of a Brahmin, or even manifesting the body of an animal. Whether during a nightmare or within a dream, or even at the moment of a sentient being’s final death, they manifest their form before the final consciousness; thereby eliminating evil karma, removing the fear of the miserable realms, and establishing them upon the wholesome paths.

That son of noble family has accomplished such inconceivable great wisdom, skillful means, and all manner of virtuous merits; having already crossed the profound great ocean of the Buddha-dharma, there is thus a wish-fulfilling jewel upon his crown.

At that time, the great assembly of those who had gathered there, witnessing this unprecedented event concerning the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Gaganagañja, all paid him profound respect with palms joined in reverence and praised him with various verses of eulogy.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Gaganagañja came forward, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How is it that the Tathāgata is able to perform the work of a Buddha amidst these sentient beings who dwell in the darkness of ignorance within this world of five turbidities?”
The Buddha told that son of good family:
"For example, space is unstained, free from affliction, and free from delusion; its nature is pure. Yet, due to the conditions of wind, rain, dust, and mist, it becomes impure.

When these conditions disperse and cease, it becomes pure as before, and one then perceives the sun, moon, and constellations, and knows the existence of kṣaṇas, lava-s, muhūrtas, days, nights, seasons, and years."
In this way, son of good family!

The Tathāgata has attained mastery over the mind through the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*). Because the minds of all sentient beings are defiled by adventitious afflictions (*āgantuka-kleśa*), the Tathāgata therefore preaches the Dharma for them, so that their defiled minds may once again attain purity.

If there are sentient beings who encounter the illumination of the Tathāgata’s wisdom, they are able to clearly understand and realize the profound Buddha-dharma—namely, the four foundations of mindfulness, the eightfold noble path, and so forth, up to abiding in the eighteen unique qualities, great loving-kindness, great compassion, and the knowledge of all modes. For this reason, Arhats, Pratyekabuddhas, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, and the Tathāgatas appear in the world.
"Good son! What do you think?
Does space depend on the eye and give rise to contact in dependence upon the eye-consciousness?"
"No, World-Honored One. "What do you think?"
“Is it that the three feelings arise based on internal eye-consciousness and conditioned by contact? “No,
World-Honored One.”
“The same applies to the ears, nose, tongue, and body.
Son of good family,
what do you think?”
“Does space depend on the mind or on mental consciousness? “No,
World-Honored One.”
“Good son, what do you think? Do sentient beings depend upon space, or does space depend upon sentient beings?”
"No, World-Honored One!
They do not depend upon one another in succession, and each has no sphere of activity; all dharmas are likewise so."
Without contemplation and without activity, they are of one single emptiness; all return to the mark of suchness, the limit of reality.
World-Honored One!

It is, for example, like space, which is without breaking, without destruction, without intrinsic nature, without marks, and without discrimination; it is also without movement, without seed, without progeny, without fruit, without retribution, and without the mark of transformation.
“World-Honored One!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva can contemplate all phenomena in accordance with such characteristics as these, this is called attaining the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena within the state of non-arising.”
He then spoke the mantra, saying:

"Tadyathā | bhadanta bha-gavan bhagavāñ chā-ma-nukṣaye naśāyaja-na-nimama-nihara-ana-naya-phala-gu-phakara-vanimamābhinaya-sa-phala-śala-pha-śala-na-śala-mana-śala-tat-kara-ma-śala-maka-ri-madhu-viśa-su-ka-śala-mali-cita-danaya-je-te-śala-tu-saṃśumbhani-nau-ki-svāhā. The Buddha said to the son of good family:
"Excellent, excellent!"

Since you are able to preach for the sake of sentient beings this Vimala-siṃhavikrāntagāmin-yāmaka-dhāraṇī, you cause all sentient beings, at the moment of their final consciousness when life ends, to be free from the hindrance of afflictions, the hindrance of karma, and the hindrance of retribution, and to attain rebirth in a pure Buddha-land.

You are able, in immeasurable and boundless lands, cities, towns, and villages—wherever people dwell—to manifest various physical forms, appearances, and modes of conduct for the sake of liberating all sentient beings through the profound Mahāyāna sūtras, enabling kṣatriyas, caṇḍāla kings, and all those who practice evil to attain wholesome dharmas.

At that time, as the World-Honored One was preaching this Dharma, immeasurable humans and devas attained samādhi, attained dhāraṇīs, and attained the various levels of patience (kṣānti), up to those who dwelt in the wisdom of the ten stages (bhūmi);
ten thousand sentient beings attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).

At that time, the bhikṣus in the great assembly, along with the devas, nāgas, humans, asuras, and others, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, were all greatly rejoiced; they paid homage and departed.
The Scripture on the Divine Incantation of the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha, in one fascicle.
